catalog_quote: East Cree words, even long ones, have one ACCENT each. ... When a vowel is accented in East Cree, it has a higher pitch. (Often, it is also louder.) ... East Cree is classified as a ‘pitch accent’ language because of the way it uses pitch. ... Words with only one vowel have an accent on that vowel. Words with two vowels can be accented on the first or last vowel. Finally, words with more than two vowels can be accented on the third-last, second-last or last vowel. ... The following rules will work for any East Cree word: Accent the second-to-last vowel if it is a tense vowel. Accent the third-to-last vowel if it is tense and if the second-last vowel is lax. However, if both the second-last and third-last vowel of the noun are lax (I, U, or A), then either vowel might be accented. For nouns, you have to memorize which vowel to accent in such cases. ... sources.quote: 'Stress differences are slight and nonphonemic, and the position of the strongest stress in the word varies freely. There is a tendency, however, for a weak stress to appear on the final syllable, except in words ending in short vowels.' (1953-54 fieldwork, one bilingual consultant; superseded by MacKenzie 1980, Brittain 2000 and Dyck & Junker 2010, all of which find rule-governed, partly contrastive accent.)

sources.note: The only full peer-reviewed metrical analysis of Southern East Cree primary stress (37 pp.); the eastcree.org Accent page, Babinski 2018 and Dyck et al. 2006 all build on it. Would let the record cite the primary analysis (final-syllable extrametricality, quantity-sensitive right-headed foot, treatment of LL sequences and of contrastive final accent) instead of the web grammar's learner-oriented rules, and settle whether the LL 'either vowel' hedge is lexical or analysable.
